title: Message Queues
overview: Message queues enable asynchronous, decoupled communication between services. A producer sends a message to a queue; a consumer processes it independently — they don't need to be running at the same time. This decoupling improves resilience (messages are durably stored), enables back-pressure handling, and allows services to scale independently based on queue depth.
keyPoints: Decouples producers from consumers — they don't need to be available simultaneously
Provides durability — messages are persisted until successfully consumed
Enables natural back-pressure and rate limiting via queue depth
Supports fan-out (one message to many consumers) and point-to-point delivery
At-least-once, at-most-once, or exactly-once delivery semantics are configurable
Dead Letter Queues (DLQ) handle messages that repeatedly fail processing

concepts.name: Point-to-Point (Queue)
concepts.description: One producer, one consumer. Each message is processed by exactly one consumer. Used for task distribution like email sending, image processing jobs.

concepts.name: Publish-Subscribe (Topic)
concepts.description: One producer, many consumers. Each subscriber receives a copy of the message. Used for event broadcast — e.g., order placed event consumed by inventory, billing, and email services.

concepts.name: At-Least-Once Delivery
concepts.description: The system guarantees each message is delivered at least once, but may deliver duplicates. Consumer must be idempotent to handle duplicate processing safely.

concepts.name: Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)
concepts.description: Messages that fail processing repeatedly are moved to a DLQ for inspection and replay. Essential for production reliability and debugging.

concepts.name: Consumer Groups
concepts.description: Multiple consumers in a group process messages in parallel from the same topic, each getting a subset of partitions. Enables horizontal scaling of consumers.

tools.name: Apache Kafka
tools.description: High-throughput distributed event streaming platform, log-based storage, ideal for event sourcing and analytics pipelines

tools.name: RabbitMQ
tools.description: Feature-rich AMQP broker with complex routing, dead letter exchanges, and priority queues

tools.name: AWS SQS / SNS
tools.description: Managed queue (SQS) and notification (SNS) services, zero infrastructure management

tools.name: Google Pub/Sub
tools.description: Globally distributed messaging with at-least-once delivery, auto-scaling, and push/pull delivery

tradeoffs: Message queues add resilience and enable async processing but introduce eventual consistency. The producer can't get an immediate response from the consumer — use request-reply patterns (correlation IDs) when synchronous confirmation is needed. Message ordering is guaranteed per partition in Kafka but not globally. Exactly-once semantics are complex and have performance overhead.
interviewTips: Kafka vs RabbitMQ: Kafka is better for high-throughput log streaming; RabbitMQ for complex routing and task queues
Always address idempotency — consumers should handle duplicate messages gracefully
Discuss ordering guarantees — Kafka guarantees per-partition order, not global order
Message queues are a key tool for handling traffic spikes without losing requests
